question.text: What is the concept of 'synthetic positions' using options?

answer.text: Creating a position that mimics the payoff of another instrument: Synthetic long stock = Long call + Short put (same strike); Synthetic short stock = Long put + Short call (same strike)
Positions created using only options with no involvement of the underlying asset
Artificial positions created by exchanges for market making purposes
Combining options from different underlyings to create a new payoff

explanation.text: The Logic: A synthetic position uses options (often with a position in the underlying or futures) to replicate the payoff of another instrument. Combining a long call and a short put at the same strike and expiry produces a payoff that mirrors being long the underlying — gains rise one-for-one above the strike and losses accumulate below it. Reversing the legs (long put + short call) replicates a short underlying position. The relationship arises from put-call parity: C - P ≈ S - PV(K), i.e. a long call/short put package behaves like a synthetic forward on the underlying. The Trap: Synthetics are not exchange-created products or regulatory constructs — they are trader-built combinations. They must use options on the same underlying (not different underlyings), and although they avoid trading the underlying directly, they aim to reproduce its payoff. Note: The NISM Series VIII (Equity Derivatives) workbook pages reviewed describe a covered call as a synthetic short put and a protective put as a synthetic long call, and cover put-call parity, but the specific identities "synthetic long stock = long call + short put" and "synthetic short stock = long put + short call" were not located in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general options-strategy industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
